curation.lead:
Landon Thomas Jr. was a financial reporter at the New York Times whose 12-year correspondence with Jeffrey Epstein -- 185 emails spanning 2007 to 2019 -- reveals one of the most fully documented cases of media capture in the Epstein record. The relationship began even earlier: in 2002, while at New York Magazine, Thomas authored the profile that became the defining public narrative of Epstein as a mysterious financier, a piece rushed to print to preempt Vicky Ward's Vanity Fair investigation. That article's framing -- complete with signaling phrases like "Russian ladies of the night" sourced from Maxwell associates -- set the template for a decade of credulous Epstein coverage. Thomas later moved to the Times, where he covered finance, sovereign wealth, and emerging-market investment while maintaining Epstein as an off-the-books source, sounding board, and patron.

The relationship was explicitly transactional in both directions. Thomas provided Epstein with advance intelligence on journalists investigating him, tipped him off about books in progress, reviewed press drafts, and reported on internal NYT newsroom events. Epstein, in return, provided Thomas with insider access to billionaires for stories -- including attempts to broker introductions to Masayoshi Son and SoftBank, Bill Gates, and Tom Barrack. Epstein also directed at least ,000 in charitable donations to Thomas's nonprofit, the Ricardo O'Gorman Garden and Center for Resources and Humanities, a Harlem Montessori preschool. The email trail captures Thomas explicitly linking his editorial output to access: "does my story on Abraaj get me a meeting with Gates next time he is in town."

Beyond the bilateral exchange, Epstein weaponized Thomas's reporting by forwarding his financial analyses to Jes Staley at JPMorgan and Barclays with instructions to "keep confidential nytimes." Thomas thus functioned as an unwitting intelligence pipeline: his professional reporting was laundered through Epstein into market-moving information for banking executives. Thomas was fired from the New York Times in 2019 after NPR exposed his solicitation of Epstein donations. The House Oversight Committee's November 2025 release of Epstein correspondence further documented the depth of their exchanges, including Epstein offering Thomas "photos of Donald and girls in bikinis in my kitchen" during the 2016 campaign.
open_questions: What was the full scope of Thomas's 2002 New York Magazine profile sourcing -- did Maxwell or her associates directly feed Thomas the 'Russian ladies of the night' framing, and was there coordination with Epstein to preempt the Ward/VF investigation?

Did Epstein direct Thomas's coverage of specific companies or financial figures, and did any of Thomas's published NYT articles contain information planted by Epstein to benefit his financial positions or network members?

Were there additional charitable donations beyond the documented $40,000 -- either to the Ricardo O'Gorman Garden or to other Thomas-affiliated organizations -- that have not yet surfaced in the EFTA or 990 records?
What was the 'other story involving a pretty senior newspaper personality' that Thomas referenced to Epstein after the Schneiderman resignation in May 2018, and why was it apparently dropped?

Did Thomas's NYT coverage of Abraaj Group, SoftBank, or Saudi royal finances reflect information or angles provided by Epstein, and were there market or political consequences from the resulting articles?

How did NYT editors become aware of Thomas's compromised status -- the October 2018 Larry Summers exclusion suggests internal suspicion predating the 2019 exposure -- and what internal review did the Times conduct of his published work?

sections.title: The Mechanics of Media Capture
sections.content:
The Thomas-Epstein relationship is significant not merely as a case of a journalist accepting gifts from a source, but as a documented example of how elite networks co-opt media coverage through structured reciprocity. The mechanism operated on multiple levels simultaneously. At the most basic level, Thomas received story tips and access to Epstein's network of billionaires -- the currency of financial journalism. At a deeper level, Epstein received something far more valuable: advance warning of incoming investigations and the ability to shape how he was portrayed.

The 2002 New York Magazine profile illustrates the pattern's origin. Thomas's piece was rushed to publication to preempt Vicky Ward's Vanity Fair investigation, which was more adversarial in its approach. The resulting article framed Epstein as an enigmatic but essentially harmless financier. Researcher Thomas Volscho characterizes this as one of several "transactional/collusion-style relationships" Epstein maintained with reporters -- a capability that "elite sex traffickers have that ordinary offenders do not." The profile's sourcing from Maxwell associates and its deployment of softening language established a narrative frame that persisted for years.

By the time Thomas was at the NYT, the arrangement had matured into a standing intelligence-exchange operation. Thomas alerted Epstein when journalist John Connolly was writing a book with James Patterson (November 2015), warned him about renewed interest in the Ken Starr hiring, flagged the Politico article on the Acosta plea deal (February 2017), and asked probing questions about the David Boies / Weinstein connection (November 2017). In each case, Thomas was providing Epstein with what intelligence professionals call "early warning" -- time to prepare responses, engage lawyers, or activate counter-narratives. Post-conviction, Thomas went so far as to pitch Epstein an NYT interview that would allow him to "define the story on your terms."

sections.title: Financial Flows Through the Ricardo O'Gorman Garden
sections.content:
The financial dimension of the Thomas-Epstein relationship was routed through the Ricardo O'Gorman Garden and Center for Resources and Humanities (EIN 13-4061835), a small Harlem Montessori preschool for at-risk children where Thomas was evidently a board member or supporter. On March 30, 2015, Thomas emailed Epstein wire instructions for a TD Bank account in the organization's name. Epstein immediately forwarded these to his financial gatekeeper Richard Kahn with a two-word instruction: "10k from foundation." This was the first confirmed payment.

A second, larger payment followed in August 2017: $30,000 from Gratitude America Ltd, Epstein's USVI-based private foundation. Thomas's email asking "what name the check would come under" suggests awareness that the money would not come directly from Epstein -- a detail consistent with the broader Epstein practice of routing payments through entity layers to obscure their origin. The total confirmed flow is at least $40,000. IRS 990 filings for the O'Gorman Garden show a steady small nonprofit whose operations were unaffected by Epstein's arrest, suggesting the conduit arrangement was episodic rather than structural.

The routing is characteristic of patterns documented across Epstein's network. Gratitude America -- which received $10,003,000 from Leon Black via BV70 LLC in October 2015 -- served as a general-purpose disbursement vehicle. The $30,000 to Thomas's charity sits alongside $525,000 to the International Peace Institute, $225,000 back to Black's Melanoma Research Alliance, and hundreds of thousands more to various recipients. The charity-to-charity routing created plausible deniability: Epstein could claim philanthropic intent, and Thomas could frame the money as a legitimate charitable gift rather than compensation for services rendered.

sections.title: The Staley Intelligence Triangle
sections.content:
One of the most structurally significant dimensions of the Thomas relationship is how Epstein used Thomas's professional output as intelligence material for third parties -- specifically Jes Staley, who served as CEO of JPMorgan's investment bank and later CEO of Barclays. In May 2010, Epstein forwarded Thomas's financial analysis directly to Staley with the annotation "keep confidential nytimes" (EFTA01300573). In a separate email, Epstein forwarded Thomas's NYT article ideas to Staley under the heading "new york times Thinkers piece" (EFTA01300609).

This information flow was not unidirectional. By August 2012, Thomas and Staley were participating in three-way email threads with Epstein, discussing the upcoming Barclays CEO succession. Thomas provided inside reporting that board chairman David Walker was favoring Antony Jenkins over Staley for the top job. Epstein then relayed this intelligence directly to Staley, writing: "as you already know the name is anthony jenkins. the story you should look at is david walker is choosing jenkins." Thomas later covered Staley's departure from Barclays in August 2017, continuing to serve as an information node in the Epstein-Staley axis even as the underlying relationship deepened.

The triangle illustrates a pattern with broader implications. Thomas believed he was cultivating a powerful source; Epstein was harvesting Thomas's professional intelligence and redistributing it to financial executives who could act on it. The "keep confidential nytimes" instruction reveals Epstein's awareness that he was handling information that had market value precisely because it came from an NYT reporter's analysis. Thomas's journalism was being laundered -- stripped of its provenance and repackaged as Epstein's own insight for consumption by bank CEOs.

sections.title: Political Intelligence Exchange During the 2016 Campaign
sections.content:
The Thomas-Epstein correspondence intensified around political subjects during the 2016 presidential campaign and its aftermath. On December 8, 2015, Epstein offered Thomas "photos of donald and girls in bikinis in my kitchen" followed by a reference to "hawaiin tropic girl lauren petrella" -- compromising material offered casually, as if the exchange of such material were routine. By May 2016, Thomas was writing to Epstein: "I am kind of shocked that our reporters did not contact you re the Trump women story. He seems to have got off rather lightly," and offered to "pass information to a political reporter" at the Times.

The intelligence flowed in both directions across multiple domains. Thomas solicited Epstein's knowledge of Trump's Wall Street finance supporters (June 2016), asked about Saudi money flows for an NYT investigation into royal family finances (October 2016), and shared Trump election analysis. Epstein, drawing on his documented Saudi connections -- including an imminent trip to Riyadh in November 2016 -- responded with institutional-grade intelligence: "most of the saudi money is tied up in pe funds. no withdrawals allowed. and im not seeing much in the secondary market." This was not gossip; it was the kind of structured financial intelligence that hedge funds pay for.

After the election, the exchange continued. In March 2017, Trump retweeted a Thomas NYT story, prompting Thomas to tell Epstein: "I think my wife is going to change the locks." In December 2017, Thomas asked about Jamie Dimon harassment rumors, and Epstein responded with a list of names: "Jamie, gates Michael Douglas, gagosian" -- a casual enumeration of powerful men and their alleged conduct that suggests Epstein maintained running files on such matters. After the Schneiderman resignation in May 2018, Thomas asked Epstein: "What about that other story involving a pretty senior newspaper personality? Dropped?" -- a reference to unreported allegations that Thomas evidently knew about through the Epstein channel.

sections.title: Access Brokering and the Masa Son Connection
sections.content:
The most explicit documentation of the quid pro quo nature of the Thomas-Epstein relationship comes from a series of 2016-2017 emails in which Thomas openly linked his editorial output to requests for access. On October 17, 2016, Thomas emailed Epstein: "does my story on Abraaj get me a meeting with Gates next time he is in town" -- a sentence that distills the entire relationship into a single transaction. His NYT coverage of Abraaj Group (a Dubai-based private equity firm that later collapsed in fraud) was framed not as journalism but as a credential to be exchanged for a meeting with Bill Gates.

The SoftBank/Masayoshi Son thread is even more revealing. On January 3, 2017, Thomas told Epstein he was doing a story on the new SoftBank tech fund and tried to arrange an Epstein introduction to the Masa/SoftBank circle. On March 3, Thomas sent his published NYT article on Masayoshi Son. Six days later, on March 9, Thomas wrote the email that most clearly documents the hybrid nature of his role: "Trying to get you in with Masa crowd. Some resistance though, due to all the headlines/controversy -- as you might expect. I tell them about your relationship with Saudis/Gates/Trump crowd but still doubts. Working on it." Here, Thomas was simultaneously acting as a reporter covering SoftBank and as a lobbyist for Epstein's social rehabilitation, deploying his NYT access to broker introductions while citing Epstein's other powerful connections as credentials.

By April 2017, the arrangement had become still more explicit: Thomas asked, "So if I offer up to Masa's bankers a meeting with Nathan would he agree to it" -- proposing to trade access to an Epstein associate (likely Nathan Myhrvold) as currency for access to Son's inner circle. The SoftBank thread demonstrates that Thomas was not merely a captured journalist but an active broker, using his editorial platform as leverage in a multilateral influence operation that served both his career advancement and Epstein's post-conviction social rehabilitation campaign.
